---
title: Edit and find notes in a Swift app
description: Rename notes offline and see how Marfa merges two changes, check a note's links as you type, and find notes by title with a filter the core writes.
---

- **You'll build** three features of Reading List: renaming a note, writing a note's text with links to other notes, and finding notes by their title.
- **You need** Reading List as [Build an app with Swift](/build/swift-app) leaves it, with its notes Bleak House and Middlemarch, and the Quickstart terminal.
- **You'll have** an app that edits notes offline, shows how Marfa settled two changes to one note, says what each link names, and keeps a search between launches.

Marfa's core does the work an app would otherwise write itself: it reads the links in a text and writes and reads filters, offline, by the same rules as the server.

<Steps paged>
<Step>

### Rename a note

Add this function inside `Library`:

```swift title="Library.swift"
    func rename(_ note: Item, to title: String) async {
        await write { copy in
            try await copy.items.update(
                note.id, Edit(properties: ["title": .string(title)], baseVersion: note.version))
        }
    }
```

The `Edit` carries the version of the note the app read, so the instance can tell whether someone else changed it since. [Write safely](/build/write-safely) explains versions from the API's side.

Add an editable row at the end of `ContentView.swift`, and replace `Text(note.title ?? "Untitled")` in `ContentView` with `NoteRow(library: library, note: note)`:

```swift title="ContentView.swift"
struct NoteRow: View {
    let library: Library
    let note: Item
    @State private var title = ""

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Title", text: $title)
            .onSubmit { Task { await library.rename(note, to: title) } }
            .onAppear { title = note.title ?? "" }
            .onChange(of: note.version) { title = note.title ?? "" }
    }
}
```

The row takes the title again whenever the note's version moves, so a change from elsewhere shows. Run the app, change Middlemarch to `Middlemarch, by George Eliot`, and press Return. **Changes** shows Sent.

</Step>
<Step>

### See a verdict

Now two devices change one note. Stop the server, rename Bleak House to `Bleak House, by Dickens`, and quit the app. The rename waits in the queue, which **survives the app quitting**.

Start the server. In the Quickstart terminal, change the same note's title as another device would, with its ID from `marfa items list --type core.note`. The note is still at version 1 on the instance:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa items update <id> --version 1 --prop title="Changed elsewhere"
```

```text
01a15f23-f2a4-7440-aeaa-46498e1819ac  core.note  2026-10-21T15:45:53.842Z  Changed elsewhere
{
  "body": "",
  "title": "Changed elsewhere"
}
```

</Terminal>

Press Command-R. The app catches up and sends the rename, and **Changes** shows **Merged title with a newer change**. The note keeps your title, because a note **keeps the last writer's title**. Had both changed the text, the instance would have kept both, yours in a conflicted copy, as [Versions](/versions) explains.

</Step>
<Step>

### Check links as you type

A note's text is Markdown, and `[[Persuasion]]` in it links to the note titled Persuasion. **When you save the text, the working copy makes a `references` edge** from the note to each note a link names. Add two functions inside `Library`, one to save a note's text and one to say what each link in a text names:

```swift title="Library.swift"
    func setText(of note: Item, to text: String) async {
        await write { copy in
            try await copy.items.update(
                note.id, Edit(properties: ["body": .string(text)], baseVersion: note.version))
        }
    }

    func links(in text: String, of note: Item) async -> [LinkCandidates] {
        let targets = linkParts(in: text).map(\.target)
        guard let copy, !targets.isEmpty else { return [] }
        return (try? await copy.items.linkCandidates(of: targets, in: note.id)) ?? []
    }
```

`linkParts(in:)` finds each link and splits it into its name, heading and alias, needing no copy, so an editor can call it on every change. `linkCandidates(of:in:)` reads the copy, with no request. A link is `bound` only where saving it would make its edge without asking the instance: by an ID the copy holds, or by a name the note already has an edge for. A copy holds a slice of your library, so it can't tell alone that one title names one note; a new link by title stays `unresolved`, with the note it found among its `candidates`, until the instance's lookup answers on save. [Links in a body](/swift-sdk/items#links-in-a-body) has the rest.

Add a sheet at the end of `ContentView.swift` that edits the text and lists its links:

```swift title="ContentView.swift"
struct TextEditorSheet: View {
    let library: Library
    let note: Item
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    @State private var text = ""
    @State private var links: [LinkCandidates] = []

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            Form {
                TextEditor(text: $text).frame(minHeight: 160)
                Section("Links") {
                    ForEach(links.indices, id: \.self) { index in
                        LabeledContent(links[index].target, value: describe(links[index]))
                    }
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle(note.title ?? "Untitled")
            .toolbar {
                Button("Save") { Task { await library.setText(of: note, to: text); dismiss() } }
            }
            .onAppear { text = note.body ?? "" }
            .task(id: text) { links = await library.links(in: text, of: note) }
        }
    }

    private func describe(_ link: LinkCandidates) -> String {
        switch link.state {
        case .bound: "Links to a note"
        case .ambiguous: "Names \(link.candidates.count) notes"
        case .unresolved: link.candidates.isEmpty ? "Names no note" : "The instance checks it on Save"
        }
    }
}
```

In `NoteRow`, add `@State private var editing = false`, and wrap the `TextField` in an `HStack` with a button that opens the sheet:

```swift title="ContentView.swift"
        HStack {
            TextField("Title", text: $title)
                .onSubmit { Task { await library.rename(note, to: title) } }
            Button("Edit Text", systemImage: "text.alignleft") { editing = true }
                .buttonStyle(.borderless)
        }
        .onAppear { title = note.title ?? "" }
        .onChange(of: note.version) { title = note.title ?? "" }
        .sheet(isPresented: $editing) { TextEditorSheet(library: library, note: note) }
```

Run the app, choose **Edit Text** on Bleak House, and type `Compare [[Middlemarch, by George Eliot]] and [[Persuasion]].` The first link says **The instance checks it on Save**, and the second **Names no note**. Choose **Save**. Once the instance answers that one note has that title, the copy makes the edge from Bleak House to Middlemarch. Choose **Edit Text** again: the first link now says **Links to a note**.

</Step>
<Step>

### Find notes by title

A listing's `filter` is text in [Marfa's filter grammar](/build/list-filter-search#filter-by-properties). Rather than write that text, build the filter from typed values and let the core write it. Add these inside `Library`:

```swift title="Library.swift"
    func find(_ text: String) {
        var filters = ListFilters(types: ["core.note"])
        if !text.isEmpty {
            let title = FilterCondition(field: .property("title"), operator: .contains, value: .text(text))
            filters.filter = try? FilterExpression(conditions: [title]).encoded()
        }
        notes?.reading = .list(filters)
        UserDefaults.standard.set(filters.filter, forKey: "filter")
    }

    var savedSearch: String {
        guard let saved = UserDefaults.standard.string(forKey: "filter"),
              let expression = try? FilterExpression(decoding: saved),
              case .text(let text)? = expression.conditions.first?.value
        else { return "" }
        return text
    }
```

`encoded()` writes the filter text, quoting the title, so a title with a quote in it can't break the filter. `FilterExpression(decoding:)` reads saved text back into conditions, the way an app edits a saved view's filter. Assigning `reading` makes the `LiveQuery` read again.

In `open()`, add `find(savedSearch)` after the line that makes `notes`, so the app opens on the last search. In `ContentView`, add `@State private var search = ""`, and these after `.navigationTitle("Reading List")`:

```swift title="ContentView.swift"
            .searchable(text: $search)
            .onAppear { search = library.savedSearch }
            .onChange(of: search) { library.find(search) }
```

Run the app and type `Bleak` in the search field. The list holds Bleak House alone. Quit the app and run it again: the search and its result are still there.

</Step>
